newsitem.title: UK: PROFIT-TAKING TO CURB ANY ITALIAN BOND ERM GAINS.
newsitem.headline: PROFIT-TAKING TO CURB ANY ITALIAN BOND ERM GAINS.

text.p: Italian bonds will get a boost if Italy's plans to reenter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) go ahead, but investors may use the chance to take profits from a year of spectacular gains, analysts said.
"There is a risk people will start to take profits," Adrian Owens, senior economist at Julius Baer in London, said on Friday.

Longer-term, the debate is open as to whether positive economic fundamentals will allow the market to continue to surge or whether a reassessment of Italy's single European currency credentials will cause investors to flee, analysts said.
EU finance ministers were due to meet in Brussels on Sunday to decide on a level at which the lira would reenter the ERM, a currency grid that sets fluctuation limits for member units.
Markets were already on the move on Friday amid talk the lira would reenter the ERM this weekend, boosting BTP futures on LIFFE and sending cash yields lower against other European debt markets.

On Friday afternoon, December BTP futures on LIFFE were quoted at 128.14, up 87 basis points on the day and the 10-year BTP/Bund cash yield spread was at 172 compared with 179 late on Thursday. The BTP/Bund gap started 1996 at around 475 basis points.
Italian bonds have surged all year on the belief that the lira would rejoin the ERM and that it may even be in the first Round of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
But analysts said many investors would use the opportunity to rack up their gains, and the spread was likely to contract another 10 basis points or so before pushing out again.

"I would have thought assuming they go in the weekend, you'll have a quick trade to 160 over and then, there will be an enormous amount of profit-taking," Mark Fox, chief European strategist in fixed income at Lehman Brothers in London.

Francesco Giordano, senior economist at San Paolo Bank in London, said markets had already largely discounted ERM membership and further bond market outperformance may depend on the central parity rate at which the lira was admitted.
Giordano said that if the lira came in at 1,000 per mark, it could be regarded by the market as too strong and cause nervousness that parity would not be sustained.
"If they come at a weaker parity, closer to 1,015, the market may take some greater comfort," he said.
The lira was quoted at 0.9842/47 per mark at 1447 GMT, having scuttled through the 1,000 barrier on Thursday.
Opinions were mixed over whether the Italian bond market could continue to forge ahead after the expected bout of profit-taking.
Owens at Baer was positive.

"The trend of spread narrowing will remain firmly on track on the back of continued good inflation prospects, lower rates and the removal of the withholding tax," he said, adding this would be key to further international support of the market.
The government is set to remove a withholding tax on bond gains early next year, he said.
He said all indications from government and bank sources was that growth and inflation prospects would be revised down, and there would be a very sharp interest rate reductions ahead.

David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London, said the party for Italian bonds would be over after the spread narrowed to 150 basis points on a last-minute re-entry surge.
"All the tail-end flows going into Italy at the moment bear all the hallmarks of a over-speculative, over-frothy, over-mature market," he said.
He said investors will soon begin to see that Italy's aspirations to join EMU were well off the mark.

According to European Commission forecasts in November, Italy will remain outside the EMU entry criteria. Its budget deficit was forecast at 3.3 percent of GDP for 1997, while the Maastricht Treaty calls for 3.0 percent and its total indebtedness to GDP will be at 122.3 percent versus a needed 60 percent. -- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
